claim: Intermediate filaments (IF) are a major component of the metazoan cytoskeleton and are essential for normal cell morphology, motility, and signal transduction.
source: Intermediate filaments (IF) are a major component of the metazoan cytoskeleton and are essential for normal cell morphology, motility, and signal transduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Dysregulation of IFs causes a wide range of human diseases, including skin disorders, cardiomyopathies, lipodystrophy, and neuropathy.
source: Dysregulation of IFs causes a wide range of human diseases, including skin disorders, cardiomyopathies, lipodystrophy, and neuropathy.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature documenting IF-related diseases.

claim: Site-specific modification of vimentin with O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) mediates its homotypic protein-protein interactions.
source: Here, we show that site-specific modification of the prototypical IF protein vimentin with O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) mediates its homotypic protein-protein interactions
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from GlcNDAz crosslinking experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Site-specific O-GlcNAcylation of vimentin is required in human cells for IF morphology.
source: Here, we show that site-specific modification of the prototypical IF protein vimentin with O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) mediates its homotypic protein-protein interactions and is required in human cells for IF morphology
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live-cell imaging of vimentin mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: Site-specific O-GlcNAcylation of vimentin is required in human cells for cell migration.
source: Here, we show that site-specific modification of the prototypical IF protein vimentin with O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) mediates its homotypic protein-protein interactions and is required in human cells for IF morphology and cell migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Transwell migration assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Chlamydia trachomatis requires specific vimentin glycosylation sites to maintain its replicative niche.
source: In addition, we show that the intracellular pathogen Chlamydia trachomatis, which remodels the host IF cytoskeleton during infection, requires specific vimentin glycosylation sites and O-GlcNAc transferase activity to maintain its replicative niche.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Chlamydia infection experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Chlamydia trachomatis requires O-GlcNAc transferase activity to maintain its replicative niche.
source: In addition, we show that the intracellular pathogen Chlamydia trachomatis, which remodels the host IF cytoskeleton during infection, requires specific vimentin glycosylation sites and O-GlcNAc transferase activity to maintain its replicative niche.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Chlamydia infection experiments with OGT inhibitor shown in Figure 5.

claim: Humans express over 70 IF proteins.
source: Humans express over 70 IF proteins, including both cytoplasmic (e.g., vimentin, keratins, neurofilaments) and nuclear (lamins) members, many with tissue-specific functions (Szeverenyi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Szeverenyi et al., 2008.

claim: All IF proteins comprise a central, conserved α-helical rod domain, as well as amino-terminal head and carboxy-terminal tail domains of varying lengths.
source: All IF proteins comprise a central, conserved α-helical rod domain, as well as amino-terminal head and carboxy-terminal tail domains of varying lengths (Lowery et al., 2015; Herrmann and Aebi, 2016; Chernyatina et al., 2015; Köster et al., 2015; Leduc and Etienne-Manneville, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: IF proteins homo- or heterodimerize through the parallel association of their rod domains into coiled coils, forming an elongated dimer of ~45–48 nm for cytoplasmic IFs and ~50–52 nm for nuclear lamins.
source: IF proteins homo- or heterodimerize through the parallel association of their rod domains into coiled coils, forming an elongated dimer of ~45–48 nm for cytoplasmic IFs and ~50–52 nm for nuclear lamins (Quinlan et al., 1986; Aebi et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Quinlan et al., 1986 and Aebi et al., 1986.

claim: IF dimers laterally associate in antiparallel fashion to form tetramers.
source: These dimers laterally associate in antiparallel fashion to form tetramers, which in turn assemble into ~65 nm unit-length filaments (ULFs) composed of eight tetramers (Herrmann and Aebi, 2016; Chernyatina et al., 2015; Herrmann et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on IF assembly.

claim: Tetramers assemble into ~65 nm unit-length filaments (ULFs) composed of eight tetramers.
source: These dimers laterally associate in antiparallel fashion to form tetramers, which in turn assemble into ~65 nm unit-length filaments (ULFs) composed of eight tetramers (Herrmann and Aebi, 2016; Chernyatina et al., 2015; Herrmann et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on IF assembly.

claim: ULFs associate end-to-end to assemble mature IFs, measuring ~10 nm across.
source: Finally, ULFs associate end-to-end to assemble mature IFs, measuring ~10 nm across (Lowery et al., 2015; Herrmann and Aebi, 2016; Chernyatina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on IF assembly.

claim: IFs are nonpolar and do not serve as tracks for molecular motors.
source: Unlike actin- or microtubule-based structures, IFs are nonpolar and do not serve as tracks for molecular motors.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about IF properties.

claim: IFs contribute to the mechanical integrity of the cell through their unique viscoelastic properties.
source: Instead, IFs contribute to the mechanical integrity of the cell through their unique viscoelastic properties (Lowery et al., 2015; Herrmann and Aebi, 2016; Chernyatina et al., 2015; Köster et al., 2015; Leduc and Etienne-Manneville, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The IF network is flexible under low strain but stiffens and resists breakage under an applied force.
source: In general, the IF network is flexible under low strain but stiffens and resists breakage under an applied force (Janmey et al., 1991; Fudge et al., 2003; Guzmán et al., 2006; Kreplak et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on IF mechanical properties.

claim: Individual IFs can be stretched up to 3.6-fold before rupture.
source: Remarkably, individual IFs can be stretched up to 3.6-fold before rupture, demonstrating their elastic nature, as compared to actin cables or microtubules (Kreplak et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kreplak et al., 2005.

claim: The IF network is highly dynamic in vivo, with IF subunits (likely tetramers) exchanging rapidly at many points along mature filaments.
source: The IF network is also highly dynamic in vivo, with IF subunits (likely tetramers) exchanging rapidly at many points along mature filaments (Mendez et al., 2010; Goldman et al., 2012; Miller et al., 1991; Vikstrom et al., 1989; Ho et al., 1998; Martys et al., 1999; Vikstrom et al., 1992; Nöding et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on IF dynamics.

claim: The IF cytoskeleton quickly reorganizes in response to numerous physiological cues, including cell cycle progression, migration, spreading, and growth factor stimulation.
source: Similarly, the IF cytoskeleton quickly reorganizes in response to numerous physiological cues, including cell cycle progression, migration, spreading, and growth factor stimulation (Lowery et al., 2015; Herrmann and Aebi, 2016; Chernyatina et al., 2015; Köster et al., 2015; Leduc and Etienne-Manneville, 2015; Yoon et al., 1998; Helfand et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Vimentin is required for mesenchymal cell adhesion, migration, chemotaxis, and wound healing in both cell culture and animal models.
source: For example, vimentin, among the most widely studied IF proteins, is required for mesenchymal cell adhesion, migration, chemotaxis, and wound healing in both cell culture and animal models (Ivaska et al., 2007; Yamaguchi et al., 2005; Eckes et al., 2000; Rogel et al., 2011; Menko et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on vimentin function.

claim: Vimentin IFs contribute to the mechanical properties of the cytoplasm.
source: Vimentin IFs also contribute to the mechanical properties of the cytoplasm, and stabilize and localize mitochondria (Nekrasova et al., 2011; Buehler, 2013; Guo et al., 2013; Eckes et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on vimentin function.

claim: Vimentin IFs stabilize and localize mitochondria.
source: Vimentin IFs also contribute to the mechanical properties of the cytoplasm, and stabilize and localize mitochondria (Nekrasova et al., 2011; Buehler, 2013; Guo et al., 2013; Eckes et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on vimentin function.

claim: Genetic lesions that dysregulate the IF cytoskeleton cause skin and nail disorders (keratins).
source: Importantly, genetic lesions that dysregulate the IF cytoskeleton cause a wide range of human diseases, including skin and nail disorders (keratins), cardiomyopathies (desmin), lipodystrophy, muscular dystrophy and progeria (lamins), giant axonal neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (neurofilaments), and cataracts (vimentin) (Omary, 2009; Omary et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Omary, 2009 and Omary et al., 2004.

claim: Genetic lesions that dysregulate the IF cytoskeleton cause cardiomyopathies (desmin).
source: Importantly, genetic lesions that dysregulate the IF cytoskeleton cause a wide range of human diseases, including skin and nail disorders (keratins), cardiomyopathies (desmin), lipodystrophy, muscular dystrophy and progeria (lamins), giant axonal neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (neurofilaments), and cataracts (vimentin) (Omary, 2009; Omary et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Omary, 2009 and Omary et al., 2004.

claim: Genetic lesions that dysregulate the IF cytoskeleton cause lipodystrophy, muscular dystrophy and progeria (lamins).
source: Importantly, genetic lesions that dysregulate the IF cytoskeleton cause a wide range of human diseases, including skin and nail disorders (keratins), cardiomyopathies (desmin), lipodystrophy, muscular dystrophy and progeria (lamins), giant axonal neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (neurofilaments), and cataracts (vimentin) (Omary, 2009; Omary et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Omary, 2009 and Omary et al., 2004.

claim: Genetic lesions that dysregulate the IF cytoskeleton cause giant axonal neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (neurofilaments).
source: Importantly, genetic lesions that dysregulate the IF cytoskeleton cause a wide range of human diseases, including skin and nail disorders (keratins), cardiomyopathies (desmin), lipodystrophy, muscular dystrophy and progeria (lamins), giant axonal neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (neurofilaments), and cataracts (vimentin) (Omary, 2009; Omary et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Omary, 2009 and Omary et al., 2004.

claim: Genetic lesions that dysregulate the IF cytoskeleton cause cataracts (vimentin).
source: Importantly, genetic lesions that dysregulate the IF cytoskeleton cause a wide range of human diseases, including skin and nail disorders (keratins), cardiomyopathies (desmin), lipodystrophy, muscular dystrophy and progeria (lamins), giant axonal neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (neurofilaments), and cataracts (vimentin) (Omary, 2009; Omary et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Omary, 2009 and Omary et al., 2004.

claim: The ectopic expression of wild type vimentin is a hallmark of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
source: In addition, the ectopic expression of wild type (WT) vimentin is a hallmark of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and is widely observed in human metastatic cancers (Satelli and Li, 2011; Nieto, 2011; De Craene and Berx, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Satelli and Li, 2011; Nieto, 2011; De Craene and Berx, 2013.

claim: Ectopic expression of wild type vimentin is widely observed in human metastatic cancers.
source: In addition, the ectopic expression of wild type (WT) vimentin is a hallmark of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and is widely observed in human metastatic cancers (Satelli and Li, 2011; Nieto, 2011; De Craene and Berx, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Satelli and Li, 2011; Nieto, 2011; De Craene and Berx, 2013.

claim: Vimentin expression levels correlate with the invasive phenotypes of breast, prostate, and other epithelial cancers.
source: IFs are likely functionally important in this context, because vimentin expression levels correlate with the invasive phenotypes of breast, prostate, and other epithelial cancers (Satelli and Li, 2011; Wei et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2011; Vuoriluoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Satelli and Li, 2011; Wei et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2011; Vuoriluoto et al., 2011.

claim: Changes in vimentin IFs are implicated in the adhesion, invasion, and replication of Chlamydia trachomatis.
source: For example, changes in vimentin IFs are implicated in the adhesion, invasion, and replication of a wide range of bacteria, including such important pathogens as Chlamydia trachomatis (Kumar and Valdivia, 2008; Jorgensen et al., 2011; Snavely et al., 2014; Bednar et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kumar and Valdivia, 2008; Jorgensen et al., 2011; Snavely et al., 2014; Bednar et al., 2011.

claim: Changes in vimentin IFs are implicated in the adhesion, invasion, and replication of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: For example, changes in vimentin IFs are implicated in the adhesion, invasion, and replication of a wide range of bacteria, including such important pathogens as Chlamydia trachomatis (Kumar and Valdivia, 2008; Jorgensen et al., 2011; Snavely et al., 2014; Bednar et al., 2011), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Garg et al., 2006; Mahesh et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Garg et al., 2006; Mahesh et al., 2016.

claim: Changes in vimentin IFs are implicated in the adhesion, invasion, and replication of Streptococcus pyogenes.
source: For example, changes in vimentin IFs are implicated in the adhesion, invasion, and replication of a wide range of bacteria, including such important pathogens as Chlamydia trachomatis (Kumar and Valdivia, 2008; Jorgensen et al., 2011; Snavely et al., 2014; Bednar et al., 2011), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Garg et al., 2006; Mahesh et al., 2016), Streptococcus pyogenes (Bryant et al., 2006; Icenogle et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bryant et al., 2006; Icenogle et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2015.

claim: Changes in vimentin IFs are implicated in the adhesion, invasion, and replication of Salmonella enterica.
source: For example, changes in vimentin IFs are implicated in the adhesion, invasion, and replication of a wide range of bacteria, including such important pathogens as Chlamydia trachomatis (Kumar and Valdivia, 2008; Jorgensen et al., 2011; Snavely et al., 2014; Bednar et al., 2011), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Garg et al., 2006; Mahesh et al., 2016), Streptococcus pyogenes (Bryant et al., 2006; Icenogle et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2015) and Salmonella enterica (Murli et al., 2001; Guignot and Servin, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murli et al., 2001; Guignot and Servin, 2008.

claim: All IFs are subject to extensive PTMs, including phosphorylation, ubiquitination, sumoylation, acetylation, farnesylation, and glycosylation.
source: Several recent lines of evidence indicate that post-translational modifications (PTMs) are an important mode of IF regulation, and indeed all IFs are subject to extensive PTMs, including phosphorylation, ubiquitination, sumoylation, acetylation, farnesylation, and glycosylation (Snider and Omary, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Snider and Omary, 2014.

claim: O-GlcNAc is an intracellular form of protein glycosylation that reversibly decorates serine and threonine residues on thousands of nuclear, cytoplasmic, and mitochondrial proteins.
source: To better understand the dynamic regulation of the IF cytoskeleton, we focused on O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc), an intracellular form of protein glycosylation that reversibly decorates serine and threonine residues on thousands of nuclear, cytoplasmic, and mitochondrial proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about O-GlcNAc.

claim: In mammals, O-GlcNAc is added by O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and removed by O-GlcNAcase (OGA).
source: In mammals, O-GlcNAc is added by O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and removed by O-GlcNAcase (OGA) (Figure 1A) (Hanover et al., 2010; Hart et al., 2011; Hart, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the enzymatic cycle.

claim: O-GlcNAc cycling controls many processes, including nutrient sensing, cell cycle progression, and apoptosis.
source: O-GlcNAc cycling controls many processes, including nutrient sensing, cell cycle progression, and apoptosis (Hanover et al., 2010; Hart et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hanover et al., 2010; Hart et al., 2011.

claim: O-GlcNAc cycling is essential, as genetic ablation of OGT or OGA is lethal in mice.
source: O-GlcNAc cycling controls many processes, including nutrient sensing, cell cycle progression, and apoptosis (Hanover et al., 2010; Hart et al., 2011), and is essential, as genetic ablation of OGT or OGA is lethal in mice (Shafi et al., 2000; Keembiyehetty et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shafi et al., 2000; Keembiyehetty et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2012.

claim: Aberrant O-GlcNAc cycling is implicated in cancer.
source: In addition, aberrant O-GlcNAc cycling is implicated in numerous human diseases, including cancer (Hart et al., 2011; Ma and Vosseller, 2013; Yi et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hart et al., 2011; Ma and Vosseller, 2013; Yi et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2015.

claim: Aberrant O-GlcNAc cycling is implicated in diabetes.
source: In addition, aberrant O-GlcNAc cycling is implicated in numerous human diseases, including cancer (Hart et al., 2011; Ma and Vosseller, 2013; Yi et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2015), diabetes (Vaidyanathan and Wells, 2014; Hardivillé and Hart, 2014; Ma and Hart, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vaidyanathan and Wells, 2014; Hardivillé and Hart, 2014; Ma and Hart, 2013.

claim: Aberrant O-GlcNAc cycling is implicated in cardiac dysfunction.
source: In addition, aberrant O-GlcNAc cycling is implicated in numerous human diseases, including cancer (Hart et al., 2011; Ma and Vosseller, 2013; Yi et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2015), diabetes (Vaidyanathan and Wells, 2014; Hardivillé and Hart, 2014; Ma and Hart, 2013), cardiac dysfunction (Erickson et al., 2013; Erickson, 2014; Dassanayaka and Jones, 2014; Darley-Usmar et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Erickson et al., 2013; Erickson, 2014; Dassanayaka and Jones, 2014; Darley-Usmar et al., 2012.

claim: Aberrant O-GlcNAc cycling is implicated in neurodegeneration.
source: In addition, aberrant O-GlcNAc cycling is implicated in numerous human diseases, including cancer (Hart et al., 2011; Ma and Vosseller, 2013; Yi et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2015), diabetes (Vaidyanathan and Wells, 2014; Hardivillé and Hart, 2014; Ma and Hart, 2013), cardiac dysfunction (Erickson et al., 2013; Erickson, 2014; Dassanayaka and Jones, 2014; Darley-Usmar et al., 2012), and neurodegeneration (Yuzwa et al., 2012; Vaidyanathan et al., 2014; Yuzwa and Vocadlo, 2014; Zhu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yuzwa et al., 2012; Vaidyanathan et al., 2014; Yuzwa and Vocadlo, 2014; Zhu et al., 2014.

claim: Numerous IF proteins are O-GlcNAcylated.
source: Interestingly, numerous IF proteins are O-GlcNAcylated (King and Hounsell, 1989; Chou et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to King and Hounsell, 1989; Chou et al., 1992.

claim: Keratin-18 glycosylation is required for the recruitment and activation of the pro-survival kinase Akt.
source: For example, keratin-18 glycosylation is required for the recruitment and activation of the pro-survival kinase Akt, and mice expressing an unglycosylatable keratin-18 mutant are sensitized to chemical injury of the liver and pancreas (Ku et al., 2010; Ku et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ku et al., 2010; Ku et al., 1996.

claim: Mice expressing an unglycosylatable keratin-18 mutant are sensitized to chemical injury of the liver and pancreas.
source: For example, keratin-18 glycosylation is required for the recruitment and activation of the pro-survival kinase Akt, and mice expressing an unglycosylatable keratin-18 mutant are sensitized to chemical injury of the liver and pancreas (Ku et al., 2010; Ku et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ku et al., 2010; Ku et al., 1996.

claim: Several neurofilament proteins are glycosylated, especially in axons.
source: Several neurofilament proteins are also glycosylated, especially in axons, and neurofilament-M O-GlcNAcylation is reduced in both human Alzheimer's disease patients and a rat model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, suggesting a potential role for dysregulated IF glycosylation in neurodegeneration (Dong et al., 1996; Dong et al., 1993; Lüdemann et al., 2005; Deng et al., 2008; Cheung and Hart, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dong et al., 1996; Dong et al., 1993; Lüdemann et al., 2005; Deng et al., 2008; Cheung and Hart, 2008.

claim: Neurofilament-M O-GlcNAcylation is reduced in both human Alzheimer's disease patients and a rat model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Several neurofilament proteins are also glycosylated, especially in axons, and neurofilament-M O-GlcNAcylation is reduced in both human Alzheimer's disease patients and a rat model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, suggesting a potential role for dysregulated IF glycosylation in neurodegeneration (Dong et al., 1996; Dong et al., 1993; Lüdemann et al., 2005; Deng et al., 2008; Cheung and Hart, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dong et al., 1996; Dong et al., 1993; Lüdemann et al., 2005; Deng et al., 2008; Cheung and Hart, 2008.

claim: Vimentin is O-GlcNAcylated on several sites, primarily in its head domain.
source: Finally, vimentin is O-GlcNAcylated on several sites, primarily in its head domain (Slawson et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Slawson et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2007.

claim: Changes in vimentin glycosylation have been observed in models of differentiating adipocytes.
source: Changes in vimentin glycosylation have been observed in models of differentiating adipocytes (Ishihara et al., 2010) and neurons (Farach and Galileo, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ishihara et al., 2010 and Farach and Galileo, 2008.

claim: Changes in vimentin glycosylation have been observed in models of differentiating neurons.
source: Changes in vimentin glycosylation have been observed in models of differentiating adipocytes (Ishihara et al., 2010) and neurons (Farach and Galileo, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ishihara et al., 2010 and Farach and Galileo, 2008.

claim: A correlation between vimentin O-GlcNAcylation and the invasive potential of cholangiocarcinoma has been observed.
source: and a recent study observed a correlation between vimentin O-GlcNAcylation and the invasive potential of cholangiocarcinoma (Phoomak et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Phoomak et al., 2017.

claim: Endogenous vimentin crosslinked into distinct, high molecular weight bands that were diazirine- and UV-dependent.
source: Endogenous vimentin crosslinked into distinct, high molecular weight bands that were diazirine- and UV-dependent (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Overexpression of OGT caused an increase in vimentin crosslinks.
source: Overexpression of OGT caused an increase in vimentin crosslinks (Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Overexpression of OGA reduced vimentin crosslinking.
source: whereas overexpression of OGA (Figure 1C) or treatment with a small molecule inhibitor of OGT, abbreviated 5SGlcNAc (Gloster et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), reduced crosslinking
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with 5SGlcNAc reduced vimentin crosslinking.
source: whereas overexpression of OGA (Figure 1C) or treatment with a small molecule inhibitor of OGT, abbreviated 5SGlcNAc (Gloster et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), reduced crosslinking
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of vimentin crosslinks obtained 80% tryptic peptide coverage of vimentin without significant enrichment of other proteins.
source: We obtained 80% tryptic peptide coverage of vimentin in these samples, without significant enrichment of other proteins, beyond common contaminants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The vimentin GlcNDAz crosslinks represent homotypic, O-GlcNAc-mediated vimentin-vimentin interactions.
source: This result suggested that the vimentin GlcNDAz crosslinks represent homotypic, O-GlcNAc-mediated vimentin-vimentin interactions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the MS proteomics data showing only vimentin in the crosslinked complexes.

claim: The GlcNDAz crosslinks of endogenous vimentin extracted into a denaturing buffer but not low or high ionic strength non-denaturing buffers, indicating that the crosslinks occur within the highly assembled filament population.
source: The GlcNDAz crosslinks of endogenous vimentin extracted into a denaturing buffer but not low or high ionic strength non-denaturing buffers, indicating that the crosslinks occur within the highly assembled filament population (Figure 1D) (Ridge et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and a citation to Ridge et al., 2016.

claim: IDPN treatment abrogated vimentin IFs and caused the accumulation of vimentin aggregates.
source: Consistent with previous reports, IDPN treatment abrogated vimentin IFs and caused the accumulation of vimentin aggregates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G) (Durham, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and a citation to Durham, 1986.

claim: IDPN suppressed the formation of GlcNDAz-dependent adducts, indicating that the crosslinks occur in assembly states beyond ULFs.
source: In the crosslinking assay, IDPN also suppressed the formation of GlcNDAz-dependent adducts, indicating that the crosslinks occur in assembly states beyond ULFs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Approximately 10% of endogenous vimentin crosslinked into GlcNDAz-dependent adducts.
source: Using quantitative IBs, we detected ~10% of endogenous vimentin crosslinked into GlcNDAz-dependent adducts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2H.

claim: O-GlcNAc-mediated vimentin-vimentin interactions are prevalent in cells, and occur primarily within assembled IFs, but not in soluble pools of lower-order assembly states.
source: Based on these results, we concluded that O-GlcNAc-mediated vimentin-vimentin interactions are prevalent in cells, and occur primarily within assembled IFs, but not in soluble pools of lower-order assembly states.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential extraction and IDPN experiments.

claim: Mutation of T33, S34, and S39 reduced vimentin crosslinking.
source: Mutation of several individual residues, including T33, S34, and S39, reduced vimentin crosslinking, while mutation of S49 abolished all detectable crosslinks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mutation of S49 abolished all detectable vimentin crosslinks.
source: Mutation of several individual residues, including T33, S34, and S39, reduced vimentin crosslinking, while mutation of S49 abolished all detectable crosslinks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: S49A mutant vimentin exhibited approximately 80% the GalNAz signal of WT, suggesting that approximately one-fifth of vimentin glycosylation occurs on S49.
source: S49A mutant vimentin exhibited ~80% the GalNAz signal of WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that approximately one-fifth of vimentin glycosylation occurs on S49 under these conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Robust and site-specific O-GlcNAcylation in the vimentin head domain mediates homotypic protein-protein interactions within IFs.
source: Together, these results suggest that robust and site-specific O-GlcNAcylation in the vimentin head domain mediates homotypic protein-protein interactions within IFs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the site-directed mutagenesis and crosslinking experiments.

claim: Cells reconstituted with WT vimentin-mEmerald exhibited canonical IF morphology.
source: Cells reconstituted with WT vimentin-mEmerald exhibited canonical IF morphology, whereas the Y117L-expressing cells lacked assembled filaments and instead displayed punctate structures consistent with ULFs (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Y117L-expressing cells lacked assembled filaments and instead displayed punctate structures consistent with ULFs.
source: Cells reconstituted with WT vimentin-mEmerald exhibited canonical IF morphology, whereas the Y117L-expressing cells lacked assembled filaments and instead displayed punctate structures consistent with ULFs (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: The S34A mutant displayed a partial defect in IF formation, with both punctate and filamentous fluorescence detected.
source: For example, the S34A mutant, which had an intermediate phenotype in our crosslinking assay (Figure 2), displayed a partial defect in IF formation, with both punctate and filamentous fluorescence detected (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The S49A mutant exhibited a significant reduction of assembled IFs in live cells, displaying a higher proportion of punctate vimentin fluorescence as compared to WT.
source: Interestingly, the S49A mutant, which lacked detectable O-GlcNAc-mediated interactions in the GlcNDAz assay (Figure 2), exhibited a significant reduction of assembled IFs in live cells, displaying a higher proportion of punctate vimentin fluorescence as compared to WT (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: The S49A mutation had no impact on vimentin stability.
source: Importantly, the S49A mutation had no impact on vimentin stability (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vimentin-S49E-expressing cells displayed a loss of filament morphology and a proportion of puncta indistinguishable from the S49A mutant.
source: Vimentin-S49E-expressing cells displayed a loss of filament morphology and a proportion of puncta indistinguishable from the S49A mutant (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The abnormal vimentin IF structures observed with the S49A mutant in live cells are due to the loss of glycosylation, not loss of phosphorylation, at S49.
source: These results suggest that the abnormal vimentin IF structures observed with the S49A mutant in live cells are due to the loss of glycosylation, not loss of phosphorylation, at S49.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the S49E phosphomimetic mutant data.

claim: Vimentin−/− cells stably transduced with empty vector or the Y117L mutant construct were impaired in serum-stimulated migration, relative to cells expressing WT vimentin.
source: Consistent with prior reports in other systems (Ivaska et al., 2007; Yamaguchi et al., 2005; Eckes et al., 2000; Rogel et al., 2011; Menko et al., 2014), vimentin−/− cells stably transduced with empty vector or the Y117L mutant construct were impaired in serum-stimulated migration, relative to cells expressing WT vimentin (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: Vimentin-S49A-expressing cells exhibited migration defects compared to WT.
source: Interestingly, vimentin-S49A-expressing cells also exhibited migration defects compared to WT (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: 5SGlcNAc treatment significantly inhibited the serum-induced migration of cells expressing WT vimentin.
source: 5SGlcNAc or Thiamet-G treatment each significantly inhibited the serum-induced migration of cells expressing WT vimentin, but not cells lacking vimentin or expressing the S49A mutant (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: Thiamet-G treatment significantly inhibited the serum-induced migration of cells expressing WT vimentin.
source: 5SGlcNAc or Thiamet-G treatment each significantly inhibited the serum-induced migration of cells expressing WT vimentin, but not cells lacking vimentin or expressing the S49A mutant (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: 5SGlcNAc and Thiamet-G did not inhibit migration in cells lacking vimentin or expressing the S49A mutant.
source: 5SGlcNAc or Thiamet-G treatment each significantly inhibited the serum-induced migration of cells expressing WT vimentin, but not cells lacking vimentin or expressing the S49A mutant (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of vimentin, especially on S49, is required for optimal serum-stimulated cell migration.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that O-GlcNAcylation of vimentin, especially on S49, is required for optimal serum-stimulated cell migration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the migration assay data with mutants and inhibitors.

claim: Chlamydia trachomatis recruits a meshwork of vimentin IFs to its vacuolar 'inclusion' compartment, stabilizing its replicative niche and shielding bacterial components from the host's cytoplasmic innate immune surveillance machinery.
source: For example, we previously showed that the obligate intracellular pathogen Chlamydia trachomatis recruits a meshwork of vimentin IFs to its vacuolar 'inclusion' compartment, stabilizing its replicative niche and shielding bacterial components from the host's cytoplasmic innate immune surveillance machinery (Kumar and Valdivia, 2008; Jorgensen et al., 2011; Snavely et al., 2014; Bednar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kumar and Valdivia, 2008; Jorgensen et al., 2011; Snavely et al., 2014; Bednar et al., 2011.

claim: 5SGlcNAc treatment inhibited the formation of a vimentin meshwork around the Chlamydia inclusion.
source: We found that 5SGlcNAc treatment inhibited the formation of a vimentin meshwork around the inclusion, consistent with a requirement for vimentin glycosylation in IF remodeling during Chlamydia infection (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 5SGlcNAc treatment reduced the average size of the inclusions in infected cells and increased the number of extra-inclusion bacteria.
source: 5SGlcNAc treatment reduced the average size of the inclusions in infected cells and increased the number of extra-inclusion bacteria (Figure 5B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: OGT activity is required for Chlamydia inclusion expansion and integrity.
source: 5SGlcNAc treatment reduced the average size of the inclusions in infected cells and increased the number of extra-inclusion bacteria (Figure 5B), demonstrating that OGT activity is required for inclusion expansion and integrity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the 5SGlcNAc treatment data in Chlamydia infection.

claim: Cells expressing either the S49A or Y117L mutant vimentin displayed reduced IF recruitment to the Chlamydia inclusions, smaller average inclusion size, and larger numbers of bacteria escaping into the cytoplasm.
source: Compared to WT vimentin-expressing cells, cells expressing either the S49A or Y117L mutant vimentin displayed reduced IF recruitment to the inclusions, smaller average inclusion size, and larger numbers of bacteria escaping into the cytoplasm (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Site-specific glycosylation of vimentin itself is required for IF remodeling during Chlamydia infection.
source: These data suggest that the site-specific glycosylation of vimentin itself is required for IF remodeling during Chlamydia infection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutant vimentin data in Chlamydia infection experiments.

claim: 5SGlcNAc had no impact on Chlamydia inclusion size or extra-inclusion bacteria in cells lacking vimentin.
source: In contrast to our observations with cells expressing WT vimentin (Figure 5A,B), 5SGlcNAc had no impact on Chlamydia inclusion size or extra-inclusion bacteria in cells lacking vimentin, indicating that vimentin, but not other host- or pathogen-encoded targets, is required for the effects of 5SGlcNAc in this context (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Vimentin, but not other host- or pathogen-encoded targets, is required for the effects of 5SGlcNAc on Chlamydia inclusion integrity.
source: In contrast to our observations with cells expressing WT vimentin (Figure 5A,B), 5SGlcNAc had no impact on Chlamydia inclusion size or extra-inclusion bacteria in cells lacking vimentin, indicating that vimentin, but not other host- or pathogen-encoded targets, is required for the effects of 5SGlcNAc in this context (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of 5SGlcNAc effects in WT and vimentin-null cells.

claim: Both OGT activity and vimentin glycosylation sites are required for IF reorganization during Chlamydia infection, and are co-opted by this pathogen to promote inclusion integrity and growth.
source: We concluded that both OGT activity and vimentin glycosylation sites are required for IF reorganization during Chlamydia infection, and are co-opted by this pathogen to promote inclusion integrity and growth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on OGT inhibition and vimentin mutants in Chlamydia infection.

claim: Portions of the vimentin head domain are required for filament assembly.
source: It is well established that portions of the vimentin head domain are required for filament assembly (Eriksson et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eriksson et al., 2004.

claim: Head domain PTMs (especially phosphorylation) govern IF dynamics in vivo.
source: and that head domain PTMs (especially phosphorylation) govern IF dynamics in vivo (Helfand et al., 2011; Eriksson et al., 2004; Chou et al., 1990; Eriksson et al., 1992; Sihag et al., 2007; Goto et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on IF regulation.

claim: Internal deletion mutations within the head domain demonstrate that S49 itself is not required for vimentin filament formation in vitro or in vivo.
source: Interestingly, however, internal deletion mutations within the head domain demonstrate that S49 itself is not required for vimentin filament formation in vitro or in vivo (Shoeman et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shoeman et al., 2002.

claim: The phenotypes observed in the S49A vimentin mutant are caused by a loss of PTM regulation, rather than simply a requirement for serine at that site.
source: Therefore, we propose that the phenotypes observed in the S49A vimentin mutant are caused by a loss of PTM regulation, rather than simply a requirement for serine at that site.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of S49 deletion and S49A mutation data.

claim: The O-GlcNAc-mediated interactions detected are likely homotypic dimeric or trimeric vimentin adducts.
source: Given the very short crosslinking radius of the GlcNDAz reagent (~2–4 Å) (Yu et al., 2012) and our MS proteomics analysis of the crosslinked complexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E), the O-GlcNAc-mediated interactions we observe are likely homotypic dimeric or trimeric vimentin adducts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the crosslinking radius and MS data.

claim: Vimentin is multiply phosphorylated.
source: Because vimentin is multiply phosphorylated (Helfand et al., 2011; Eriksson et al., 2004; Chou et al., 1990; Eriksson et al., 1992; Sihag et al., 2007; Goto et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on vimentin phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphatase treatment of crosslinked adducts had no effect on their SDS-PAGE migration.
source: and phosphatase treatment of crosslinked adducts had no effect on their SDS-PAGE migration (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The discrete bands in the GlcNDAz-induced vimentin complexes represent different crosslinking geometries of vimentin multimers.
source: Instead, we postulate that the discrete bands in the GlcNDAz-induced vimentin complexes represent different crosslinking geometries of vimentin multimers.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the crosslinking data.

claim: An individual glycan on the vimentin head domain may contact the head domain of its dimeric partner, and/or the rod domain of a vimentin molecule in an adjacent dimer, and/or another vimentin molecule within the same ULF.
source: Because the O-GlcNAc-mediated interactions we detect occur primarily in assembled IFs (Figure 1D,E), an individual glycan on the vimentin head domain (e.g., at residue S49) may contact the head domain of its dimeric partner, and/or the rod domain of a vimentin molecule in an adjacent dimer, and/or another vimentin molecule within the same ULF.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about possible crosslinking geometries.

claim: O-GlcNAc mediates specific contacts among vimentin molecules, and not a large variety of nonspecific interactions.
source: Irrespective of the molecular identities of the individual adducts, the fact that we observe a highly reproducible crosslinking pattern suggests that O-GlcNAc mediates specific contacts among vimentin molecules, and not a large variety of nonspecific interactions, which would produce variable or smeared crosslinking (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the reproducible crosslinking pattern and citation to Yu et al., 2012.

claim: The head domain of vimentin is intrinsically disordered.
source: This evidence of specific contacts is perhaps surprising, given the widely accepted model that the head domain of vimentin is intrinsically disordered (Guharoy et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guharoy et al., 2013.

claim: In vivo, O-GlcNAcylation may mediate site-specific contacts between glycans on one vimentin molecule and discrete glycan recognition sites or domains on adjacent vimentin molecules within assembled filaments.
source: It is possible that, in vivo, O-GlcNAcylation mediates site-specific contacts between glycans on one vimentin molecule and discrete glycan recognition sites or domains on adjacent vimentin molecules within assembled filaments.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of O-GlcNAc-mediated interactions.

claim: Vimentin has a GlcNAc-binding property on the cell surface.
source: Interestingly, several prior reports identified a GlcNAc-binding property of vimentin on the cell surface (Ise et al., 2010; Ise et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012; Komura et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ise et al., 2010; Ise et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012; Komura et al., 2012.

claim: Two mutations in vimentin that abolish extracellular GlcNAc binding, E382A and E396A, do not reduce intracellular GlcNDAz crosslinking.
source: However, two mutations in vimentin that abolish extracellular GlcNAc binding, E382A and E396A (Komura et al., 2012), do not reduce intracellular GlcNDAz crosslinking (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Komura et al., 2012.

claim: The intracellular O-GlcNAc-mediated interactions are distinct from the reported glycan-binding property of cell surface vimentin.
source: Therefore, our observations are distinct from the reported glycan-binding property of cell surface vimentin (Ise et al., 2010; Ise et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012; Komura et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the E382A and E396A mutant data.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation at S34, S39, or S49 influences the assembly and/or disassembly of vimentin filaments.
source: At the cellular level, specific glycosylation sites of vimentin, including S34, S39 and especially S49, are essential for IF morphology and for facilitating serum-stimulated migration (Figures 3 and 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 3). We propose that O-GlcNAcylation at one or more of these sites influences the assembly and/or disassembly of vimentin filaments, as has been described for other PTMs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutant phenotype data.

claim: Phosphorylation of several residues in the vimentin head domain promotes IF disassembly in response to multiple stimuli.
source: Indeed, phosphorylation of several residues in the vimentin head domain promotes IF disassembly in response to multiple stimuli (Helfand et al., 2011; Eriksson et al., 2004; Chou et al., 1990; Eriksson et al., 1992; Sihag et al., 2007; Goto et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on vimentin phosphorylation.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation and phosphorylation often compete for nearby or identical residues on specific protein substrates.
source: O-GlcNAcylation and phosphorylation often compete for nearby or identical residues on specific protein substrates, giving rise to a complex functional interplay between these PTMs (Hart et al., 2011; Butkinaree et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hart et al., 2011; Butkinaree et al., 2010.

claim: S34 and S39 can be phosphorylated.
source: Moreover, specific O-GlcNAc sites required for in vivo IF assembly in our work, such as S34 and S39 (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), can also be phosphorylated (Helfand et al., 2011; Eriksson et al., 2004; Chou et al., 1990; Eriksson et al., 1992; Sihag et al., 2007; Goto et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on vimentin phosphorylation.

claim: Reciprocal PTMs at S34 or S39 may have antagonistic effects, with glycosylation promoting IF assembly, while phosphorylation induces disassembly.
source: Therefore, reciprocal PTMs at certain sites may have antagonistic effects, with glycosylation of S34 or S39 promoting IF assembly, while phosphorylation at those sites induces disassembly.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the known interplay between O-GlcNAc and phosphorylation.

claim: S49 is not a reported phosphorylation site.
source: In contrast, vimentin S49 is required for normal IF assembly in human cells (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and is a known glycosylation site (Slawson et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2007) but is not a reported phosphorylation site.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of S49 in phosphorylation literature.

claim: (De)glycosylation of S49 is required for WT levels of cell migration and pathogen-induced IF remodeling.
source: Taken together, these results strongly indicate that (de)glycosylation of S49 is required for WT levels of cell migration and pathogen-induced IF remodeling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on S49 mutants and OGT inhibition.

claim: Chlamydia deploys the CPAF protease to dismantle the IF cytoskeleton and promote bacterial release at late stages of infection.
source: Chlamydia remodels the IF cytoskeleton to stabilize the inclusion during its replication phase, and deploys the CPAF protease to dismantle the IF cytoskeleton and promote bacterial release at late stages of infection (Kumar and Valdivia, 2008; Jorgensen et al., 2011; Snavely et al., 2014; Bednar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kumar and Valdivia, 2008; Jorgensen et al., 2011; Snavely et al., 2014; Bednar et al., 2011.

claim: WT levels of CPAF-mediated vimentin cleavage were detected with the S49A and Y117L mutants.
source: We detected WT levels of CPAF-mediated vimentin cleavage with the S49A and Y117L mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that the phenotypes we observe are not due to differential vimentin cleavage during infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The phenotypes observed in Chlamydia infection with S49A and Y117L mutants are not due to differential vimentin cleavage during infection.
source: We detected WT levels of CPAF-mediated vimentin cleavage with the S49A and Y117L mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that the phenotypes we observe are not due to differential vimentin cleavage during infection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the CPAF cleavage data.

claim: Numerous IF proteins are dynamically glycosylated in vivo.
source: In addition, our work may have broad implications for other IF proteins. Numerous IF proteins are dynamically glycosylated in vivo (King and Hounsell, 1989; Chou et al., 1992; Ku et al., 2010; Dong et al., 1996; Dong et al., 1993; Lüdemann et al., 2005; Deng et al., 2008; Cheung and Hart, 2008; Slawson et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2007; Srikanth et al., 2010; Kakade et al., 2016; Tao et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on IF glycosylation.

claim: The S49 residue of vimentin is conserved both among vertebrate vimentin orthologs and in human desmin.
source: and the S49 residue of vimentin is conserved both among vertebrate vimentin orthologs and in human desmin, another type III IF protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Site-specific O-GlcNAcylation may be a general mode of regulating IF dynamics and function.
source: Therefore, site-specific O-GlcNAcylation may be a general mode of regulating IF dynamics and function.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the conservation of S49 and widespread IF glycosylation.

claim: Pharmacological modulation of O-GlcNAcylation may provide a way to manipulate filament form and function for therapeutic benefit in diseases of dysregulated IFs.
source: In the future, pharmacological modulation of O-GlcNAcylation may provide a way to manipulate filament form and function for therapeutic benefit in diseases of dysregulated IFs, ranging from neurodegeneration and cardiomyopathy to cancer.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic applications.
